identity.title: Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze (60 s)

technique.how: Seated, measure or note the baseline lid position (margin-reflex distance). Ask the patient to fix on a target held above eye level and hold upgaze for 60 s (some protocols 2 min) without blinking hard. Positive if one or both lids progressively droop during upgaze and recover after a period of eye closure/rest.
technique.prerequisites: Adequate light, patient able to cooperate and hold gaze; note asymmetry and compensatory brow elevation.

interpretation.positive_finding: Progressive drooping of the eyelid during sustained upgaze that improves with rest supports ocular myasthenia (sensitivity about 0.80 in a referral clinic). Combine with Cogan lid twitch, orbicularis weakness, diplopia history, or an ice-pack test for stronger rule-in.
interpretation.negative_finding: A stable lid over 60 s lowers but does not exclude MG (about 20% of OMG patients had no fatigability); antibody testing and single-fiber EMG remain necessary when suspicion persists.
interpretation.pitfalls: Specificity is modest (0.63): aponeurotic ptosis and tired patients can show apparent fatigue; mild ptosis in eyes with low lid folds may not fatigue visibly; the reference study included this sign in its diagnostic definition (incorporation bias).
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: check for bulbar/respiratory weakness and send AChR antibodies, consider ice-pack test and neurology; negative with normal motility and pupils: MG unlikely, consider aponeurotic ptosis.

estimates.population: 138 patients referred to an academic neuro-ophthalmology clinic for suspected MG (101 with MG, 95 ocular); retrospective
estimates.reference_standard: Clinical OMG (isolated ptosis/diplopia) supported by >=1 abnormal test (edrophonium, ice, lid twitch, upgaze fatigability, AChR antibody, RNS or SFEMG); composite that includes the index sign
estimates.quote: Test sensitivity/specificity in OMG was fatigability on sustained upgaze 0.80/0.63

sources.citation: Scherer K, Bedlack RS, Simel DL. Does this patient have myasthenia gravis? JAMA. 2005;293(15):1906-1914.
Mittal MK, Barohn RJ, Pasnoor M, et al. Ocular myasthenia gravis in an academic neuro-ophthalmology clinic: clinical features and therapeutic response. J Clin Neuromuscul Dis. 2012;13(1):46-52.
Kee HJ, Yang HK, Hwang JM, Park KS. Evaluation and validation of sustained upgaze combined with the ice-pack test for ocular myasthenia gravis in Asians. Neuromuscul Disord. 2019;29(4):296-301.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use to triage a patient with dyspnea, dysphagia or neck weakness: suspected myasthenic crisis needs vital capacity/SBC and monitoring irrespective of lid findings.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Ptosis with new diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia or breathlessness: assess respiratory function immediately (FVC, NIF, single breath count) and involve neurology.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Lid position change is judged visually; measured MRD change (>=2 mm) improves reproducibility. Estimate derives from a retrospective referral cohort with incorporation bias, so real-world accuracy is probably lower.

extraction_notes: The 2005 JAMA RCE (PMID 15840866) did not identify studies of sustained-upgaze fatigability, so it is cited as series anchor only. The single accuracy estimate is from the abstract of Mittal 2012 (PMID 22361625): sensitivity 0.80 / specificity 0.63 in a retrospective neuro-ophthalmology referral cohort; LRs and prevalence computed by extractor from abstract numbers (computed=true). Incorporation bias: upgaze fatigability was one of the tests allowed to define OMG. Kee 2019 (PMID 30704861) evaluates the ice-pack test performed after 2 min sustained upgaze (sensitivity 73.3%, specificity 96.7% vs 43.3%/100% conventional) - a different index test, so not entered as an estimate for this record. Sustained-upgaze duration in the source cohort is not stated in the abstract; the 60 s in the title is convention.
